                    ### Question
                    A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of dry cough and low-grade fever. Four months ago, she was diagnosed with major depressive disorder and started treatment with fluoxetine. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A diagnosis of upper respiratory infection is made and a medication is prescribed to relieve her symptoms. A drug with which of the following mechanisms of action should be avoided in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Disruption of mucoid disulfide bonds
opb. Inhibition of H1 receptors
opc. Reduction in secretion viscosity
opd. Inhibition of NMDA glutamate receptors
ope. Stimulation of α-adrenergic receptors

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
In this case, the patient is on fluoxetine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), which can increase serotonin levels. The risk of serotonin syndrome arises when additional serotonergic agents are introduced. Therefore, drugs that inhibit NMDA glutamate receptors (option opd) could potentially increase serotonin levels and should be avoided. The other options do not present a direct conflict with fluoxetine: inhibition of H1 receptors (option opb) is common in antihistamines and does not interact negatively with fluoxetine; disruption of mucoid disulfide bonds (option opa) and reduction in secretion viscosity (option opc) are mechanisms of mucolytics that are safe; and stimulation of α-adrenergic receptors (option ope) can cause increased blood pressure but is not contraindicated with fluoxetine. Thus, the most concerning mechanism of action to avoid in this patient is the inhibition of NMDA glutamate receptors.
